fact: Plaster of Paris is obtained by calcining **gypsum**.
detail: CaSO_{4}·2H_{2}O heated to 120–160 °C gives CaSO_{4}·½H_{2}O. Sets in 5–10 minutes.

fact: Early strength of cement → **C_{3}S**. Ultimate strength → **C_{2}S**. Highest heat of hydration → **C_{3}A**.
detail: C_{3}S ~40–50%, C_{2}S ~25–30%, C_{3}A ~8–12%, C_{4}AF ~6–10%. C_{4}AF gives colour and little strength.

fact: Gypsum (3–5%) **retards** setting — it increases the setting time by preventing a flash set of C_{3}A.
OPC setting time: initial **not less than 30 min**, final **not more than 600 min** (10 h).
detail: Low heat cement is allowed 60 min initial. Measured on the Vicat apparatus.

fact: Vicat apparatus → consistency and setting time. **Le Chatelier apparatus → soundness.**
detail: Fineness → 90 μm sieve or Blaine. Strength → 70.6 mm mortar cubes.

fact: Primary raw material for cement is **limestone** (supplies 60–65% CaO). Main hydration product is **C-S-H gel**.
Strength of cement **decreases** on storage: ~20% in 3 months, 30% in 6, 40% in 12.
**White cement** is used for painting and decorative finishes — low iron oxide content.
detail: Fe_{2}O_{3} is what makes ordinary cement grey; keeping it below ~0.4% leaves it white.

fact: Brick earth: silica 50–60%, alumina 20–30%, lime ≤5%, iron oxide 5–6%, magnesia <1%.
detail: Sand/silica **prevents warping, shrinking and cracking**; excess makes it brittle. Alumina gives plasticity; excess causes shrinkage. **Iron oxide gives the red colour** — excess turns it dark blue/black, deficiency pale yellow.

fact: The indentation on a brick face is the **frog**; it is laid facing **upward**.
detail: Typically 100 × 40 × 10–20 mm. Omitted on wire-cut and flooring bricks.

fact: Brick compressive strength: first class **10.5 N/mm²**, second class 7.0, third class 3.5.
detail: Test with the frog filled flush with **1:1** cement–sand mortar, loaded at 14 N/mm²/min.

fact: Brick water absorption (24 h): **not more than 20%** for first class; 15% for class 12.5 and above; 22% second class.
detail: Collections quoting "0.15" are a mistyped 15%. A 0.15% absorption is impossible for burnt clay.

verification.notes: Source key gave "0.15"; the standard limit is 20% by weight for a first class brick.

fact: **Bloating** = swelling of a brick from trapped gases. **Efflorescence** = white alkali salt patches. **Lamination** = laminae from trapped air.
Burning develops brick strength; drying only removes moisture so it does not crack when burnt.
detail: Order: clay preparation → moulding → drying → burning.

fact: Metamorphic pairs: sandstone→**quartzite**, limestone→**marble**, shale→**slate**, granite→**gneiss**.
detail: Quartzite is chemically **siliceous**. Slate is argillaceous; marble and limestone are calcareous.

fact: **Hydraulic lime** (5–30% clay) is used in lime mortar — it sets under water. Fat lime (<5% clay) sets only in air.
detail: Poor lime has >30% clay. Slaking = adding water to quicklime CaO → Ca(OH)_{2}, exothermic.

fact: Seasoning of timber = **reducing moisture content**. Drawback of electrical seasoning is **splitting**.
detail: Target 10–12% interior, 15–18% exterior. Fungi need ~20% to attack.

fact: Fibreboard density: hardboard >800, **medium 350–800**, low (insulation) <350 kg/m³.
detail: Some collections quote medium density as 600–800 or 960 kg/m³. 960 is firmly hardboard.

verification.notes: Source gave "600 to 800, prefer 960". IS 3348 puts medium density at 350–800 kg/m³.

fact: Paint: **pigment gives colour**; base gives body; vehicle (linseed oil) binds; thinner (turpentine) makes it workable; drier speeds oxidation.
detail: **Red lead** is the pigment for corrosion resistance on structural steel.

fact: **Lacquer is a spirit varnish** — shellac in alcohol, dries by evaporation, not weather resistant.
**Plastic bitumen is used for crack filling.** Cutbacks: RC (naphtha), MC (kerosene), SC (diesel).
detail: Blown/oxidised bitumen → roofing, pipe coating. Tar comes from destructive distillation of coal; bitumen is a petroleum residue.

fact: Ore dressing order: crushing → **concentration** → calcination/roasting → smelting → refining.
detail: **Washing** removes clay adhering to iron ore. Calcination excludes air; roasting uses excess air to remove sulphur.

verification.notes: Source key gave "pressing" for removal of clay from iron ore. Pressing is a metal-forming operation; the ore-dressing step is washing.

fact: Carbon: wrought iron <0.25%, **steel 0.15–1.5%**, cast iron 2–4%. Stainless steel's main alloying element is **chromium** (12–18%).
detail: More carbon → harder, stronger, more brittle, less weldable.

fact: **Ductility** = drawn into wire. **Malleability** = beaten into sheets. **Toughness** = absorbs impact. **Hardness** = resists scratching.
**Shoring** temporarily supports an unsafe structure. **Underpinning** strengthens a foundation. **Scaffolding** is a working platform.
detail: Shore types: raking (45°–75°), flying (between two walls), dead (vertical, with needles).

fact: **Hacking** = roughening a surface before plastering. Plaster coats: rendering → floating → finishing.
detail: Before plastering: rake out joints, clean, roughen and thoroughly wet the surface.

fact: **Number of treads = number of risers − 1.** Comfort rule 2R + T ≈ 600 mm.
detail: Residential: rise 150–190 mm, tread 250–300 mm. Max ~12–15 risers per flight.

fact: Dress stone **immediately after quarrying**, while the quarry sap keeps it soft — then season it 6–12 months before use.
Moment of inertia: rectangle bd³/12 (centroid), **bd³/3 (base)**; triangle bh³/36 (centroid), bh³/12 (base), **bh³/4 (vertex)**.
detail: Vertex value is **9×** the centroidal value for a triangle. Ratios 1 : 3 : 9.

fact: Circle **πd⁴/64**; hollow circle **π(D⁴−d⁴)/64**; semicircle about diameter **πd⁴/128** = πR⁴/8.
detail: Polar J = π(D⁴−d⁴)/32 — twice the diametral value. Z of hollow circle = π(D⁴−d⁴)/(32D).

fact: Centroids from base: solid hemisphere **3r/8**, hemispherical shell r/2, semicircular lamina **4r/3π**, cone and pyramid **h/4**, triangle h/3.
Radius of gyration **k = √(I/A)**; I = Ak². Slenderness ratio λ = l_{e}/k.
detail: For a rectangle about its centroid, k = d/√12 = 0.2887d.

fact: **Perpendicular axis theorem (plane laminae only): I_{zz} = I_{xx} + I_{yy}.** Parallel axis theorem: I = I_{G} + Ah².
detail: For a circular lamina, I_{zz} = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32 — the polar moment used in torsion.

fact: **Plinth area estimate** = plinth area × rate from a similar building. **Cubical content** = plinth area × height × rate — more accurate.
detail: Carpet area ≈ **50–65%** of plinth area. Plinth area ≈ 60–75% of plot area under typical bye-laws.

fact: **Rate analysis** builds the rate per unit of work: materials + labour + plant + overheads + profit (~10–15%).
detail: Distinguish from **valuation** (present worth of an existing property) and **specification** (required quality of materials and workmanship).

fact: **Steel** is the preferred formwork material for repeated reuse — 100–2000+ uses versus 8–10 for timber.
Bulking of sand peaks at **4–6% moisture** (20–40% volume increase) and is **zero at full saturation**.
detail: Sand batched by volume must be corrected for bulking or the mix will be sand-deficient.

fact: NDT on concrete: rebound hammer, ultrasonic pulse velocity, pull-out, cover meter, half-cell potential. The **cube compression test is destructive**.
The fundamental principle of surveying is **working from whole to part**.
detail: Accurate control first, detail afterwards — so errors are **localised rather than accumulated**, and every stage carries a built-in check. The second principle: fixing a point needs **two independent measurements** from a known base.

fact: **BB − FB = ± 180°.** A departure from 180° means **local attraction** at one of the two stations.
detail: Local attraction affects **all bearings from a station equally**, which is what makes it correctable: find a line whose FB and BB do differ by 180°, and work outwards from it. Do not confuse it with **magnetic declination**, which exists everywhere.
The prefix alternates **N, S, S, N** and the suffix goes **E, E, W, W**. So a WCB of 200° is **S 20° W**.

fact: **Rise and fall** check: **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** — three quantities that must agree.
detail: **Height of collimation** has only two of those checks, so it **does not verify intermediate sights**. Use collimation for many detail levels (faster), rise and fall for precise work (fully checked).

fact: Combined **curvature and refraction correction = 0.0673 d²** metres, with d in km.
detail: Curvature alone is 0.0785d² (makes objects appear **lower**); refraction restores about **1/7** of it. Negligible at 100 m, **67 mm at 1 km** — which is why back and fore sight distances are kept **equal**, and why **reciprocal levelling** is needed across a wide river.

fact: **Contours cannot cross — except at an overhanging cliff**, and cannot merge except at a **vertical cliff**.
detail: **V pointing uphill = valley** (contours point upstream); **U or V pointing downhill = ridge**. Close contours mean steep ground; a closed contour with **higher values inside** is a hill, with lower values a depression.

fact: Observing on **both face left and face right** eliminates **collimation and trunnion axis** errors.
detail: **Both verniers** remove **eccentricity of centres**; **repetition** removes **graduation** error. Nothing removes a **non-vertical vertical axis** — the instrument must simply be levelled properly.

fact: **Tacheometry: D = Ks + C**, with **K = f/i = 100** and **C = 0** for an anallatic lens.
detail: Inclined sight, staff vertical: **D = Ks cos²θ + C cos θ**, **V = Ks(sin 2θ)/2**. Accuracy about **1 in 500–1000**, so tacheometry is for **detail and contouring**, never the primary control.

fact: **Bowditch rule** distributes closing error in proportion to **line length** (compass traverse); **transit rule** in proportion to **latitude/departure** (theodolite traverse).
detail: **Closing error e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]**, expressed as a **relative** error against the perimeter. Balancing **hides** error — if the misclosure exceeds the permissible limit, **re-observe** rather than distribute it.

fact: **Simpson's rule needs an ODD number of ordinates** (even number of intervals); the **trapezoidal rule accepts any number**.
detail: **Simpson: (d/3)[first + last + 4(even) + 2(odd)]** — more accurate for a curved boundary. Its volume analogue is the **prismoidal formula**; the difference from the trapezoidal result is the **prismoidal correction**.

fact: **A total station measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and SLOPE distance** — everything else it reports is computed.
detail: **GNSS needs four satellites** for a 3D fix, because the receiver clock error is a fourth unknown alongside X, Y, Z. Total station needs **line of sight**; GNSS needs **sky view** — so they are complements, not rivals.

fact: **Degree of curve: R ≈ 1719/D** on the **30 m chord** definition (**1146/D** for a 20 m chord).
detail: From R = 57.3C/D. **Rankine's deflection angle δ = 1718.9 C/R minutes.** The **first and last sub-chords are shorter** than the standard chord and need their own deflection angles — the commonest setting-out error.

fact: Plane tabling: **radiation** and **intersection** fix **detail**; **traversing** fixes **stations**; **resection** fixes **the observer's own position**.
detail: The **three-point problem** solves resection, but fails if the station lies on the **danger circle** through the three known points, where the position is indeterminate. **Chain correction: true length = measured × (wrong chain length ÷ true length)** — a stretched chain reads **short**.
